variants.title: Turn a snapshot into a corpus
variants.context: A source snapshot becomes a corpus through four stages: register and quarantine the bytes, extract and classify documents, curate and protect with explicit gates, then mix and publish a frozen recipe. Each stage records why it kept or dropped a document.
variants.prompt: A team has just downloaded a new web archive snapshot and wants a trainable corpus version from it. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Curate and protect: apply quality, safety, privacy, deduplication, opt-out, and evaluation-overlap gates with explicit decision reasons.
Extract and classify: decode formats, preserve metadata, segment documents, identify language, and quarantine malformed payloads.
Register and quarantine the snapshot: record origin, retrieval time, permission basis, checksums, retention policy, and a stable source ID.
Mix and publish: choose source weights, tokenize deterministically, emit slice statistics, sign the manifest, and freeze the recipe.

variants.hint: Which stage has to know the permission basis before any bytes are processed?
variants.explanation: Permission and provenance are established at acquisition, so every later gate and every published shard can be traced back to a registered source.

variants.title: Turn a snapshot into a corpus
variants.context: A source snapshot becomes a corpus through four stages: register and quarantine the bytes, extract and classify documents, curate and protect with explicit gates, then mix and publish a frozen recipe. Each stage records why it kept or dropped a document.
variants.prompt: An encrypted archive lands in the pipeline and never becomes tokens. Put the stages it reaches in order, ending where it stops.

items.text: The payload is quarantined as malformed rather than passed downstream.
The curation ledger records the quarantine reason so accepted plus rejected still reconciles with input.
Extraction tries to decode the format and fails to segment any document.
The archive is registered with its origin, checksum, and permission basis under a stable source ID.

variants.hint: A document that cannot be parsed still owes the ledger an answer.
variants.explanation: Quarantine is a recorded decision, not a silent drop, because the count invariant has to hold for every input document.

variants.title: Turn a snapshot into a corpus
variants.context: A source snapshot becomes a corpus through four stages: register and quarantine the bytes, extract and classify documents, curate and protect with explicit gates, then mix and publish a frozen recipe. Each stage records why it kept or dropped a document.
variants.prompt: Two source families are being combined for one release. Put the work in order from acquisition to a signed release.

items.text: Source weights are chosen, tokenization runs deterministically, and slice statistics are emitted.
The manifest is signed and the complete recipe is frozen for the training run.
Documents from each snapshot are extracted, segmented, and labeled with a language.
Quality, privacy, deduplication, and evaluation-overlap gates run with a recorded reason per document.
Both snapshots are registered separately with their own retention policies and source IDs.

variants.hint: Mixture weights are a release decision, not an acquisition decision.
variants.explanation: Weights are chosen after the surviving population per source is known, and freezing the recipe is what makes the run reproducible.

variants.title: Protect the benchmarks
variants.context: Benchmark families and private test sets are reserved before training data is assembled, decontamination compares candidates against that held-out content before the split is finalized, and the check reruns whenever the evaluation inventory or the corpus recipe changes.
variants.prompt: A new model will be scored on three public benchmark families and one private test set. Put the decontamination work in order.

items.text: Block known exact matches and reviewed near matches from entering the training split.
Reserve the benchmark families and the private test set before any training data is assembled.
Compare candidate documents against that held-out content while the corpus is still being curated.
Finalize the training split and record the contamination check in the manifest.

variants.hint: Which artifact has to exist before the comparison can mean anything?
variants.explanation: Reserving evaluation content first is what makes the comparison honest, because a benchmark chosen after the split cannot prove the model never saw it.

variants.title: Protect the benchmarks
variants.context: Benchmark families and private test sets are reserved before training data is assembled, decontamination compares candidates against that held-out content before the split is finalized, and the check reruns whenever the evaluation inventory or the corpus recipe changes.
variants.prompt: Two new benchmarks are added to the evaluation inventory a month after the corpus was published. Put the response in order.

items.text: Republish the corpus version with the newly blocked documents removed and the check recorded.
Add the two benchmarks to the reserved evaluation inventory.
Rerun the contamination check against the published corpus using the new held-out content.
Review the near matches the check surfaces and decide which are genuine overlap.

variants.hint: The trigger here is a change in the evaluation inventory, not a change in the data.
variants.explanation: Contamination checks rerun whenever the evaluation inventory or the corpus recipe changes, because either change can create overlap that the earlier check could not see.

variants.title: Protect the benchmarks
variants.context: Benchmark families and private test sets are reserved before training data is assembled, decontamination compares candidates against that held-out content before the split is finalized, and the check reruns whenever the evaluation inventory or the corpus recipe changes.
variants.prompt: An ablation changes the extraction code and the near-duplicate threshold, so the corpus is rebuilt. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Rebuild the document population under the changed recipe.
Publish a new corpus version whose manifest names the changed code and threshold.
Rerun the contamination check against the reserved evaluation content on the rebuilt population.
Finalize the new training split only after the check clears.
Version the new extraction code and the new threshold as part of the recipe.

variants.hint: A changed recipe produces a different document population, so an old clearance does not transfer.
variants.explanation: Decontamination is a property of a specific recipe and population, so a rebuilt corpus needs its own check before the split is finalized.

variants.title: Reconcile the curation ledger
variants.context: The curation invariant is stronger than proving the filter ran: accepted plus rejected counts must equal the input count, and every decision must be reproducible from a versioned rule or model.
variants.prompt: A curation run reports 12,400,000 input documents, 9,150,000 accepted, and 3,150,000 rejected. How many documents have no recorded decision?
variants.hint: Compare the two reported buckets against the input count.
variants.explanation: Accepted plus rejected must equal input, so a gap of 100,000 means the run cannot be released until every document has a recorded decision.

mistakes.feedback: That is the rejected count the invariant demands, not the number of documents missing a decision.
Assuming the ledger balances is the failure the invariant exists to catch; add the reported buckets and compare them to the input.

variants.title: Reconcile the curation ledger
variants.context: The curation invariant is stronger than proving the filter ran: accepted plus rejected counts must equal the input count, and every decision must be reproducible from a versioned rule or model.
variants.prompt: A low-resource language slice enters curation with 480,000 documents and 336,000 are accepted. What percentage of that slice was rejected?
variants.hint: The rejected share is what the input count leaves after the accepted count.
variants.explanation: Per-slice acceptance and rejection rates are what expose a global threshold that treats one language far more harshly than another.

mistakes.feedback: That is the acceptance rate; the question asks for the rejected share.
That is the rejected document count, not the percentage of the slice.

variants.title: Reconcile the curation ledger
variants.context: The curation invariant is stronger than proving the filter ran: accepted plus rejected counts must equal the input count, and every decision must be reproducible from a versioned rule or model.
variants.prompt: A dedup stage takes in 6,000,000 documents. Exact hashes remove 900,000, normalized hashes remove a further 450,000, and near-duplicate clustering removes another 1,050,000. How many documents survive dedup?
variants.hint: Each method runs on what the previous one left.
variants.explanation: Exact, normalized, and near-duplicate methods catch different populations, so the surviving count is the input minus every stage's removals.

mistakes.feedback: Only the exact-hash removals were subtracted; the later stages remove documents too.
The near-duplicate stage was left out of the subtraction.

variants.title: Place the concern in the contract
variants.context: The corpus contract has five boundaries: purpose names the capabilities and languages, permission records license and consent constraints, quality defines measurable acceptance rules, evaluation reserves held-out benchmarks, and reproducibility versions snapshots, code, checkpoints, thresholds, and weights.
variants.prompt: A new corpus contract is being drafted. Match each boundary to what it must state.

pairs.label: Purpose boundary
pairs.detail: Names the model capabilities and languages the corpus is meant to support.

pairs.label: Permission boundary
pairs.detail: Records license, contract, consent, opt-out, retention, and geography constraints per snapshot.

pairs.label: Quality boundary
pairs.detail: Defines measurable acceptance rules plus review samples for accepted and rejected documents.

pairs.label: Evaluation boundary
pairs.detail: Reserves benchmark families and private test sets before training data is assembled.

pairs.label: Reproducibility boundary
pairs.detail: Versions source snapshots, extraction code, classifier checkpoints, thresholds, and mixture weights.

variants.hint: Ask what each boundary would stop you from doing if it were missing.
variants.explanation: The contract turns a vague request for more data into five testable requirements, each of which can be audited independently.

variants.title: Place the concern in the contract
variants.context: The corpus contract has five boundaries: purpose names the capabilities and languages, permission records license and consent constraints, quality defines measurable acceptance rules, evaluation reserves held-out benchmarks, and reproducibility versions snapshots, code, checkpoints, thresholds, and weights.
variants.prompt: Four incidents surface during a corpus review. Match each incident to the boundary it violates.

pairs.label: A benchmark item appears verbatim in a published token shard
A licensed archive was used past its agreed retention window
The classifier checkpoint used for filtering was overwritten and the run cannot be rebuilt
Nobody can say which languages the corpus was supposed to serve

variants.hint: Name the promise each incident breaks before naming the boundary.
variants.explanation: Every incident maps to one boundary, which is why the contract is written before collection rather than reconstructed after a failure.

variants.title: Place the concern in the contract
variants.context: The corpus contract has five boundaries: purpose names the capabilities and languages, permission records license and consent constraints, quality defines measurable acceptance rules, evaluation reserves held-out benchmarks, and reproducibility versions snapshots, code, checkpoints, thresholds, and weights.
variants.prompt: A second review raises four more findings. Match each finding to the boundary it belongs to.

pairs.label: The acceptance threshold is a number in a notebook with no stated rule or review sample
A user opt-out cannot be honored because derived copies were never traced
A new benchmark was added after the training split was already frozen
The mixture weights for the last release were never written down

variants.hint: Two findings here are about being unable to prove what you did, and they are not the same boundary.
variants.explanation: Untraceable permissions and unrecorded weights fail different boundaries, which is why lineage and versioning are tracked separately.

variants.title: Audit a global gate
variants.context: Quality filtering and deduplication are model decisions, not neutral cleanup. A global threshold can reject dialects, code-switching, short reference answers, or smaller languages at a higher rate, and aggressive near-deduplication can collapse legitimate templates, translations, and rare variants.
variants.prompt: A single global quality threshold rejects 78 percent of a code-switched Hindi and English slice while rejecting 19 percent of the monolingual English slice. What should the team do first?
options: Keep the threshold because it is applied identically to every document in the corpus.
Review accepted and rejected samples from the code-switched slice before keeping the threshold.
Drop the code-switched slice and record the coverage gap in the corpus manifest.
optionFeedback: Uniform application is exactly what produces uneven rejection, so it is not evidence that the gate is fair.
Reading real accepted and rejected examples from the harmed slice is what shows whether the gate is measuring quality or measuring style.
Dropping the slice makes the capability gap permanent without ever testing whether the gate was wrong.
variants.hint: The threshold is a model decision, so ask what evidence would show it is measuring the right thing.
variants.explanation: Per-slice review of accepted and rejected samples is the check that separates a quality gate from a dialect filter.

variants.title: Audit a global gate
variants.context: Quality filtering and deduplication are model decisions, not neutral cleanup. A global threshold can reject dialects, code-switching, short reference answers, or smaller languages at a higher rate, and aggressive near-deduplication can collapse legitimate templates, translations, and rare variants.
variants.prompt: After near-duplicate clustering, a reviewer finds that 40 human translations of one public policy page collapsed into a single surviving document. What does this indicate?
options: The clustering worked, since the translations carry the same underlying content.
The clustering is too aggressive and is removing legitimate multilingual variants.
The translations were contaminated and should also leave the evaluation set.
optionFeedback: Treating translations as redundant copies is how a dedup gate quietly removes a language from the corpus.
Collapsing legitimate translations is the known cost of aggressive near-deduplication and needs a threshold review per slice.
Nothing here connects the translations to held-out benchmark content, so contamination is the wrong diagnosis.
variants.hint: Ask whether the collapsed documents were really the same evidence or the same meaning.
variants.explanation: Near-deduplication reduces repeated exposure but can collapse templates, translations, and rare variants, so its effect is measured per slice.

variants.title: Audit a global gate
variants.context: Quality filtering and deduplication are model decisions, not neutral cleanup. A global threshold can reject dialects, code-switching, short reference answers, or smaller languages at a higher rate, and aggressive near-deduplication can collapse legitimate templates, translations, and rare variants.
variants.prompt: A minimum document length gate is removing almost every dictionary entry and short reference answer from a curated source. What is the right response?
options: Move the short entries into the evaluation set since they are too small to train on.
Raise the length gate further so only long, clearly substantial documents survive.
Measure the gate per source and set an acceptance rule that fits short reference material.
optionFeedback: Evaluation content is reserved for measurement, so moving rejected training documents there corrupts the benchmark.
Raising the gate deepens the same bias and removes more of the material the source was acquired for.
A gate tuned per source keeps short reference answers that a single global length rule would silently discard.
variants.hint: Ask whether length is a proxy for quality in this particular source.
variants.explanation: A global rule inherits the shape of whichever source it was tuned on, so acceptance rules are measured and set against each source's real documents.
